newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND HAS MIXED REVIEWS AT EU PARLIAMENT MEETING.
newsitem.headline: POLAND HAS MIXED REVIEWS AT EU PARLIAMENT MEETING.

text.p: Poland gained warm support for its EU membership bid on Tuesday, along with advice to hasten the adjustment of its laws, at a meeting in Warsaw of a committee grouping European and Polish parliamentarians.

"I can say the atmosphere in the European Parliament (EP) is very favourable to the entry of Poland to the European Union," said EP deputy from Austria Ursula Stenzel, joint head of the Polish-EU parliamentary commission.
"Poland is seen as the country which is most important when it comes to expanding the EU at the moment," she told a news conference after meeting President Aleksander Kwasniewski.

But on the first day of the Monday-Wednesday meeting, the EU's ambassador in Warsaw Rolf Timans said Poland was taking too long to adjust its laws to make them compatible with those of the union and was going more slowly than promised.
This could bear on an assessment by the Union's executive commission of its readiness to begin entry talks, he said.
Timans told Reuters on Tuesday such delays were not due to ill-will but because of Poland's concentration on laying new economic and other foundations for its future.
"They have a double task -- creating a sound basis for their future and on top of that comes this enormous body of rules and regulations deriving from European integration policies," he said.
"They will absolutely have to speed up, that is for sure," Timans added.
Poland expects to start entry talks six months after the end of the EU's Inter-governmental conference this year.

It officially hopes to join the Union around the year 2000 and has got pledges of support for this target from Germany and France, but German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel on Monday recognised that around 2002 was the earliest realistic date.
Poland's Rzeczpospolita newspaper reported him as telling a a Polish-German forum in Bonn that Poland was among the leading entry candidates, but the procedures could not be speeded up.
The joint parliamentary committee, formed in 1993, meets twice a year, alternating between Warsaw and Brussels.
